project.name: fibcalc
project.description: FibCalc is a high-performance Go calculator for arbitrarily large Fibonacci numbers, built as an academic prototype that demonstrates Clean Architecture, zero-allocation sync.Pool strategies, adaptive parallelism, and PGO. It implements Fast Doubling, Matrix Exponentiation with Strassen, FFT-based multiplication (Schoenhage-Strassen), and an optional GMP backend, with a Bubble Tea TUI dashboard. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

nodes.name: context.go

nodes.name: fftmulToCtx
nodes.summary: Internal helper that converts x/y into polynomials via the bump allocator and calls mulCachedWithBumpCtx, then materialises the product back into dst.

nodes.summary: Internal squaring counterpart of fftmulToCtx that reuses a single polynomial through sqrCachedWithBumpCtx.

nodes.name: transformWithBumpCtx
nodes.summary: Performs the forward Schönhage-Strassen Fourier transform using fermat-slice and word-slice bump allocations and delegates the recursion to fourierWithBumpCtx.

nodes.name: invTransformWithBumpCtx
nodes.summary: Inverse Fourier transform with bump allocator, scaling by N^{-1} and shifting via fermat representation; returns a nat suitable for downstream IntTo.

nodes.name: mulCachedWithBumpCtx
nodes.summary: Pointwise polynomial multiplication using cached forward transforms for both operands plus an inverse transform, all routed through the bump allocator.

nodes.name: fft.go
nodes.summary: Top-level Schönhage-Strassen multiplication entry points (Mul/MulTo/Sqr/SqrTo) with atomic FFT-threshold tuning and a post-condition-aware recover policy that re-panics fermat-invariant violations instead of masking them as errors.

nodes.name: Mul

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to see the story FibCalc tells about itself: an academic prototype that computes arbitrarily large Fibonacci numbers at extreme speed. It introduces the four algorithms you will meet in this tour (Fast Doubling, Matrix Exponentiation, Schönhage-Strassen FFT, and an optional GMP backend) and the engineering pillars that make them fast (sync.Pool recycling, bump allocator, adaptive parallelism, PGO). The rest of the tour walks the same path through the actual code, so keep this document open as a map.

tour.title: CLI Entry Point
tour.description: The fibcalc binary's main() is intentionally trivial: it constructs an Application, calls Run, and translates an ExitAction into the process exit code. All real wiring lives one layer in, in internal/app — keeping cmd/ as a thin shim is a deliberate Clean Architecture choice that lets internal packages stay un-importable from outside the module.
tour.languageLesson: Go's 'internal' directory is a compiler-enforced boundary: anything under internal/ can only be imported by code rooted at the parent of that internal/ directory. Putting cmd/fibcalc/main.go at the top and pushing logic into internal/app makes the public surface of the module a single binary.

tour.title: Application Lifecycle & Dispatch
tour.description: internal/app/app.go is the wiring hub: it parses config, then routes to one of four modes (completion, calibration, TUI, or calculate). calculate.go is the production hot path — it validates the memory budget, installs timeout and signal contexts, then hands off to orchestration. This is where the four layers of Clean Architecture meet: config below, orchestration sideways, fibonacci/bigfft deeper, and presentation (cli/tui) above.
tour.languageLesson: Go's context.Context is the idiomatic way to propagate cancellation, timeouts, and signal handling down a call stack. Pairing context.WithTimeout with signal.NotifyContext gives you Ctrl-C and deadline cancellation through the same channel, which is how a long Fibonacci computation gets cleanly interrupted.

tour.title: Configuration: Flags, Env, Hardware
tour.description: AppConfig is the single struct that flows through the entire application. config.go registers CLI flags and orchestrates validation; env.go layers in environment overrides; hardware.go probes runtime.NumCPU and system memory to produce sensible defaults; thresholds.go picks initial FFT/parallel/Strassen cutoffs that calibration will later refine. The .env.example file documents every knob a user can turn.

tour.title: Orchestration: Concurrent Algorithm Runs
tour.description: When the user asks for a comparison run, the orchestrator selects calculators (one or many), launches them concurrently under an errgroup with a bounded semaphore, and aggregates progress through a single ProgressAggregator. AnalyzeComparisonResults then summarizes the multi-algorithm output. This layer is where bounded parallelism enters the picture before the math layers see it.
tour.languageLesson: golang.org/x/sync/errgroup combines a sync.WaitGroup with first-error capture and a shared context.Context — when one goroutine fails, the context cancels and the rest unwind cleanly. It is the standard Go idiom for 'run N concurrent tasks, surface the first error, cancel the rest'.

tour.title: The Calculator Façade & Strategy Family
tour.description: calculator.go defines FibCalculator, the public façade that wraps any CoreCalculator with shared concerns: memory budgeting, GC suspension, FFT cache wiring, and progress observation. strategy.go declares the narrow Multiplier and DoublingStepExecutor interfaces, and ships two implementations: AdaptiveStrategy (routes between schoolbook, Karatsuba, and FFT based on operand size) and FFTOnlyStrategy (forces FFT, useful for benchmarks). registry.go provides name-based factory lookup so flags like --algo fast resolve to the right implementation.
tour.languageLesson: Go interfaces are structural and intentionally small (ISP: 'many small interfaces beat one big one'). Multiplier has one method — Mul. DoublingStepExecutor has one method too. Composition of these narrow contracts is what lets AdaptiveStrategy and FFTOnlyStrategy be swappable without a single type assertion in the hot path.

tour.title: Fast Doubling: The Hot Path
tour.description: fastdoubling.go is the most sensitive file in the codebase. It implements the default O(log n) algorithm using the identity F(2k) = F(k)·(2·F(k+1) − F(k)) and concentrates the package's hardest invariants: a pooled CalculationState that owns its arena, an alias-detachment step that must run unconditionally before returning the state to the pool, and a panic-safe GC suspension via WithGC. doubling_framework.go is the generic driver — it walks N's bits MSB-down, delegating squarings and multiplications to a Multiplier and asking a DynamicThresholdManager whether each step should run sequentially or in parallel.
tour.languageLesson: sync.Pool is Go's standard answer to GC pressure for short-lived allocations. The catch: when a pooled object owns slices that alias into a shared arena, you must zero those aliases before Put — otherwise the next consumer sees stale data. The TestReleaseState_OverLimit_AliasesCleared test exists precisely to guard that invariant.

tour.title: Alternative Algorithms: Matrix, FFT-Only, GMP
tour.description: The same DoublingFramework backs three additional CoreCalculators. matrix.go computes Fibonacci via 2x2 matrix exponentiation (with Strassen kicking in past a Strassen threshold). fft_based.go forces FFT-domain multiplication for every step — slower for small N but invaluable for benchmarking and correctness checks against Fast Doubling. calculator_gmp.go is gated by the gmp build tag and binds to GNU MP via CGO for a different speed/portability trade. Together they form the algorithmic family the README promises.
tour.languageLesson: Go build tags (e.g. //go:build gmp) gate files at compile time. calculator_gmp.go only enters the build when you pass -tags=gmp, which lets the project ship a pure-Go default and a CGO-linked fast path from the same source tree without a single runtime branch.

tour.title: Schönhage-Strassen FFT Kernel
tour.description: internal/bigfft is the math kernel beneath every algorithm that ends up multiplying very large big.Ints. fft.go exposes Mul/MulTo/Sqr/SqrTo with an atomic FFT-threshold and a recover policy that re-panics fermat invariant violations instead of masking them as errors. fft_recursion.go runs the recursive FFT with adaptive parallelism (atomic-tuned recursion threshold, max-depth cap, bounded semaphore). fermat.go implements arithmetic in the Fermat ring Z/(2^n+1), where every panic is an intentional invariant check — not error handling, but a contract violation alarm.
tour.languageLesson: atomic.Int64 and atomic.Pointer[T] give you lock-free reads and writes on shared scalars. They replaced plain globals in bigfft to remove a data race in tuning paths — the hot path can now read fftThreshold thousands of times per second without contending with a mutex.

tour.title: Memory Engineering: Pools, Bump, Arena, GC Control
tour.description: This is the engineering that turns asymptotic complexity into wall-clock speed. bump.go gives O(1) linear allocation for FFT temporaries with no fragmentation. pool.go runs size-classed sync.Pool families per buffer kind, with capacity-based routing and a miss counter that surfaces pool churn. fft_cache.go is a thread-safe LRU of polynomial Fourier transforms — a 15-30% speedup on repeated squarings, with a putByKey policy that always allocates a fresh backing buffer to prevent aliasing on eviction. arena.go and gc_control.go close the loop on the Fibonacci side: per-calculation slab allocation and a panic-safe wrapper that disables the GC for N ≥ 1M and guarantees restoration.
tour.languageLesson: Go's runtime.GC()/debug.SetGCPercent(-1) lets you turn the garbage collector off entirely. That's an extreme optimization only worth it for short, allocation-heavy bursts — and it must be wrapped in a panic-safe defer so a crash never leaves the GC permanently off. WithGC(fn) encodes exactly that contract.

tour.title: Adaptive Thresholds & Calibration
tour.description: Static thresholds would be wrong on most hardware. threshold/manager.go (the DTM) tracks per-iteration timings via atomic.Int64 fields and an atomic.Pointer[time.Time], then nudges the FFT and parallel thresholds at runtime — all lock-free for the hot path. The calibration subsystem runs micro-benchmarks once (or on demand), persists a versioned CalibrationProfile to disk with a hardware fingerprint, and rejects stale profiles routed through CompleteStrategy. Together they make the same binary fast on a laptop and on a 24-core workstation.
tour.languageLesson: Go's sync/atomic package, used through the typed atomic.Int64/atomic.Pointer[T] wrappers introduced in Go 1.19, replaces the older pattern of unsafe pointer arithmetic. The DTM stores the entire hot-path tuning state in atomics, so reads cost a single MOV instruction and writes never block.

tour.title: Interactive TUI Dashboard
tour.description: The --tui flag launches a btop-style live dashboard built with Bubble Tea. model.go is the Elm Architecture root: a pure Update router that dispatches messages to header/logs/metrics/chart/footer sub-models. bridge.go is the load-bearing adapter between the production progress/result interfaces and Bubble Tea's message bus — note that the TUI never imports internal/fibonacci directly, only the orchestration.Calculator aliases, a layering boundary enforced by TestArchitectureLayering.
tour.languageLesson: The Elm Architecture (Model-View-Update) imported into Go by Bubble Tea forces state changes to flow through a single pure Update(msg) function. No goroutine ever touches the Model directly — they send messages over a channel — which is why the entire TUI works correctly under -race without a single mutex inside the model.

tour.title: Validation Surface: Makefile, Golden Corpus, Container
tour.description: FibCalc has no CI/CD — local discipline is the only safety net, so the Makefile is the sole validation entry point: make test runs the race detector, make benchmark runs the perf suite, make lint runs 24 golangci-lint linters, make build-pgo produces a PGO-optimized binary. fibonacci_golden.json is the immutable oracle (now including F(50000), F(100000), F(200000)) that every algorithmic test consults for non-regression — extending it requires explicit ADR approval. The Dockerfile demonstrates the production packaging path: a CGO-enabled builder stage on golang:1.26-bookworm with libgmp-dev, and a distroless runtime stage that consumes default.pgo when present.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use multiple FROM statements: a heavy builder image with the compiler and CGO dependencies (libgmp-dev), and a minimal runtime image (distroless/base-debian12, nonroot user) that only copies the final binary. The result is a small, attack-surface-reduced image even though the build needed gigabytes of toolchain.
